generatedProse.concept-context: Psychology students meet reflective models often, especially on practicals and placements, where you are asked to reflect on how a session or a study went. A simple three-stage model gives that reflection a shape: describe what happened in the session or task, reflect on why it went that way, and decide what to change. It keeps a psychology logbook or reflective commentary from becoming a mere diary of events.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students use the three-stage model to reflect on the same research methods group task that did not go well.

Tom writes: 'Our group presentation on the study design was rushed and we ran over. It was stressful. I hope the next one goes better.' This describes the experience and names a feeling, but it stops there. It offers no real reflection on why it was rushed, and the 'hope' is not an action. Two of the three stages are missing.

Amara works through all three. Describe: 'We ran over and had to skip our discussion of confounds.' Reflect: 'We ran over because we never timed a practice run, and we had divided the design, results and critique without agreeing who presented what, so we overlapped. Our critique of the confounds was actually strong.' Take action: 'Next time we will do one timed practice run and agree who speaks to each section.' This is the full model: a fair description, an honest assessment of good and bad, and a specific action.

Both reflected on the same task. Only Amara moved through all three stages, so only Amara came away with something to do differently.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, a simple reflective model has three stages: describe what happened in the task or session, reflect on why and what you make of it, and take action by deciding what to do differently. You can now describe the three stages, give an example of each, and recognise which stage a reflective statement belongs to. The next lesson looks at what keeps a reflection honest and balanced.

check.body: In the worked example, which part of Amara's reflection is the 'take action' stage?

items.text: Deciding to do a timed practice run and agree who speaks to each section.
Stating that the group ran over and skipped the confounds.
Explaining that they overlapped because roles were not agreed.
Noting that the critique of the confounds was strong.

feedback.correct: That's right. Deciding what to do differently is the take action stage.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Which part says what Amara will do differently next time?
feedback.incorrectFinal: The take action stage is deciding on a timed practice run and agreed roles. Stating what happened is describe, and working out why is reflect.
